newsitem.title: NEW ZEALAND: NZ Bolger says Maori TV funding an obligation.
newsitem.headline: NZ Bolger says Maori TV funding an obligation.

text.p: New Zealand Prime Minister Jim Bolger on Tuesday defended Cabinet's decision to pump another $4 million into a pilot Maori television broadcaster, saying it was an obligation of the government under the Treaty of Waitangi.

"The funding of Maori broadcasting comes out of court decisions flowing from the Treaty of Waitangi so there is no debate about supporting Maori broadcasting on radio and television. It is a question of getting the right formula," Bolger told journalists.
He said the pilot would be funded until the end of the financial year in June. Then the whole question of delivering the government's obligations to Maori language television could be addressed.

Cabinet on Monday decided to provide $2 million for Aotearoa Television and direct another $2 million to be provided by broadcasting funding agency New Zealand On Air. It has faced criticism from Opposition MPs and some of its own backbenchers, who said it had bowed to pressure from Maori in National's coalition partner, New Zealand First.
Bolger and Communications Minister Maurice Williamson raised the possibility of using a revamped, partly commercial TV1 or the TVNZ regional network to meet the government's commitments.
Labour leader Helen Clark said that during failed coalition talks with NZ First last year NZ First had wanted state-owned TVNZ to be directed to sell off its regional stations.
Williamson told journalists even more money would be required once a final decision was made on the shape of Maori language television after June 30.

"What we will have to face is a considerably bigger sum of money ... From July 1 on we will not be talking about $4 million, we will be talking of a considerable size of money" but the amount would be determined by how the broadcasts were delivered, Williamson said as he went into a National caucus meeting.
Williamson said there were obligations under the Treaty determined by the courts and work was under way to establish a long term vehicle for delivering Maori language television.

"We are not bailing out anyone. Television has an unbelievable capacity to consume large chunks of dollars," Williamson said, adding he could not understand the programmes on Aotearoa TV but had been told by Maori elders it was of good quality. -- Wellington newsroom 64 4 473 4746
